Optimizing training performance in large language models (LLMs) remains an essential challenge, particularly in improving model performance while maintaining computational costs. This work challenges the conventional approach of training LLMs using next-token prediction (NTP), arguing that by predicting information-rich tokens during training, there is a more effective way to train LLMs. We investigate the impact of the proposed solution in three kinds of tasks for LLMs: arithmetic, multi-label classification of text, and natural-language generation. This work offers a principled approach to optimizing LLM training, advancing both model performance and theoretical understanding of the target-token selection strategies.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Consistently Simulating Human Personas with Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning

Marwa Abdulhai, Ryan Cheng, Donovan Clay, Tim Althoff, Sergey Levine, Natasha Jaques

NeurIPS 2025

/neurips/2025/abdulhai2025neurips-consistently/

## Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human users in interactive settings such as therapy, education, and social role-play. While these simulations enable scalable training and evaluation of AI agents, off-the-shelf LLMs often drift from their assigned personas, contradict earlier statements, or abandon role-appropriate behavior. We introduce a unified framework for evaluating and improving persona consistency in LLM-generated dialogue. We define three automatic metrics—prompt-to-line consistency, line-to-line consistency, and Q\&A consistency—that capture different types of persona drift and validate each against human annotations. Using these metrics as reward signals, we apply multi-turn reinforcement learning to fine-tune LLMs for three user roles: a patient, a student, and a social chat partner. Our method reduces inconsistency by over 55%, resulting in more coherent, faithful, and trustworthy simulated users.

# Beyond Next Token Prediction: Patch-Level Training for Large Language Models

Chenze Shao, Fandong Meng*, Jie Zhou  
Pattern Recognition Center, WeChat AI, Tencent Inc, China  
{chenzeshao,fandongmeng,withtomzhou}@tencent.com

## ABSTRACT

The prohibitive training costs of Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a significant bottleneck in the development of next-generation LLMs. In this paper, we show that it is possible to significantly reduce the training costs of LLMs without sacrificing their performance. Specifically, we introduce patch-level training for LLMs, in which multiple tokens are aggregated into a unit of higher information density, referred to as a ‘patch’, to serve as the fundamental text unit for training LLMs. During patch-level training, we feed the language model shorter sequences of patches and train it to predict the next patch, thereby processing the majority of the training data at a significantly reduced cost. Following this, the model continues token-level training on the remaining training data to align with the inference mode. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Published 11/4/2025 by Chun-Hao Yang, Bo-Han Feng, Tzu-Yuan Lai, Yan Yu Chen, Yin-Kai Dean Huang, SHOU-DE LIN

## Overview

  * Large language models currently train by predicting one token at a time, which may waste potential learning signals
  * The paper proposes focusing training on information-rich tokens rather than treating all tokens equally
  * Information-rich tokens contain more meaningful information about the output and require more reasoning to predict
  * This approach aims to improve model efficiency and performance by concentrating learning effort where it matters most
  * The research tests this strategy on arithmetic tasks and other domains where certain tokens carry more predictive weight

4 Experimental Methodology

We investigate the consistency of LLM-based simulated human agents across three interactive

domains: open-ended conversation, education, and mental health. While consistency is important

for user trust and effective communication in open-ended conversational settings, it is especially

critical in domains like education and mental health, where downstream agents—such as teachers or

mental health counselors—must be trained against stable, realistic human behavior to develop reliable

education and mental health tools. Our experiments are designed to answer three key questions:

(1) Do our automated metrics align with human judgments of consistency? (2) How consistent are

current LLM simulators across diverse dialogue contexts? (3) Can multi-turn reinforcement learning

improve simulator consistency to support more effective downstream training?
